dialogue:
A: So, I’ve been diving into the fascinating world of white blood cells lately. You know, those little warriors in our bloodstream?

B: Oh, totally! The white blood cell count, right? I mean, it's like the ultimate health report card for our immune system. 

A: Exactly! So, a white blood count measures how many of these leukocytes we have in our blood, which is super important because they’re the ones fighting off infections and stuff.

B: Right! And if you’re sick, your body cranks out more of these guys. I mean, it’s like an army getting ready for battle! 

A: Haha, yes! And then, if you’re healthy, it’s between, like, 4,000 and 11,000 cells per microliter of blood. Can you imagine if we had to count them all? 

B: Oh man, that would take forever! I’d be like, “Uh, can I get a calculator for this?” 

A: Seriously! And it’s kind of wild how different ages and conditions can affect those numbers. Kids usually have more white blood cells than adults, right?

B: Yep! It’s like their immune systems are on hyperdrive. But if someone has a low count, that can be a sign of bigger issues, like infections or even some cancers.

A: Exactly! It’s like your body’s SOS signal. And then there’s the opposite end of the spectrum, where you have a high count, which can indicate autoimmune diseases or, you know, infections.

B: And let’s not forget about the different types of white blood cells—like neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, monocytes, and basophils! Each has its own specialty, like a superhero team!

A: Oh, for sure! I can just imagine them in capes, each fighting their own battles. “You handle the bacteria, I’ll take care of the viruses!” 

B: Haha! And then there’s the blood differential test, which breaks down how many of each type you have. It’s like a detailed report on your immune system's performance!

A: Totally! So, like, if you're feeling unwell, a doctor will usually order a WBC count as part of a complete blood count, right?

B: Yup, and it’s such a crucial diagnostic tool. You really can learn a lot about what’s happening inside your body just by looking at those numbers.

A: I mean, it’s pretty amazing how much our blood can tell us. But enough about our immune system—did you catch any of the World Baseball Classic scores lately?

B: Oh, switching gears to baseball! I love it! No, what’s the latest? 

A: Well, I’ve heard the games are heating up, and it’s getting intense! 

B: Sweet! I can’t wait to check them out. I just love the excitement of international competition. 

A: Same here! It’s like a whole different vibe, right? The energy from the fans is just electric!

B: For sure! So, should we keep an eye on those scores while we geek out over white blood cells? 

A: Sounds like a plan! But, you know, I might need a score update every few minutes! 

B: Haha, no problem! Let’s keep the health talk rolling while we cheer for our favorite teams!

SOURCE TITLE: White Blood Count (WBC): MedlinePlus Medical Test
SOURCE CONTENT: What is a white blood count (WBC)?
A white blood count measures the number of white blood cells (WBCs) in your blood. White blood cells, also called leukocytes, are part of your immune system. They are a type of blood cell made in your bone marrow and found in your blood and lymph tissue (part of your immune system). If you are injured or get sick, the white blood cells will travel through your bloodstream and tissues to where they are needed. There, they will help your body fight off infections and other diseases.
When you get sick, your body makes more white blood cells to fight the bacteria, viruses, or other foreign substances causing your illness. This increases your white blood count.
Other diseases can cause your body to make fewer white blood cells than you need. This lowers your white blood count. Diseases that can lower your white blood count include some types of cancer and HIV, a viral disease that attacks white blood cells. Certain medicines, including chemotherapy, may also lower the number of your white blood cells.
There are five major types of white blood cells:
- Neutrophils
- Lymphocytes
- Monocytes
- Eosinophils
- Basophils
A white blood count measures the total number of these cells in your blood. Another test, called a blood differential, measures the amount of each type of white blood cell.
Other names: WBC count, white cell count, white blood cell count, Leukocyte Count, WBC
What is it used for?
A white blood count is most often used to help diagnose or monitor disorders related to having a high white blood cell count or low white blood cell count.
Disorders related to having a high white blood count include:
- Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, conditions that cause the immune system to attack healthy tissues
- Bacterial or viral infections
- Cancers such as leukemia and Hodgkin disease
- Allergic reactions

What is a white blood cell count?
Our blood contains a certain white blood cell count (WBC, leukocytes or leucocytes) which, as part of the body’s immune system, help the body fight infection. 1 A white blood cell (WBC) count measures the amount of white blood cells in a sample of a person’s blood. The number of white blood cells in the body differs between individuals or at different ages in their lives. The normal white blood cell count in a healthy adult is between 4,000 and 11,000 WBCs per microliter (μl or mcL) or cubic millimeter (mm3) of blood, though this may differ between males and females, and healthy children and young people usually have more.
Feeling unwell?
To measure the number of white blood cells in a person’s body, a doctor will order a white blood cell count, often as part of a complete blood count (CBC) test. A low white blood cell count can indicate conditions including infections, inflammation, certain cancers, HIV/AIDS, and others, making it an important diagnostic test. Aside from these conditions, a person’s white blood cell count can indicate their immune system activity, response to cancer treatment and overall health.
What are white blood cells (WBCs)?
There are several kinds of white blood cells (WBCs), including neutrophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes, monocytes and basophils. Each variety plays a different role in protecting the body from foreign pathogens such as viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites. White blood cells also defend the body from allergens, mutated cells, such as cancer, and foreign matter, such as splinters, and remove dead cells, old red blood cells and other debris. 1
A white blood cell count checks both the overall levels of white blood cells in the blood, as well as the overall proportion of different types of white blood cells.
